newsitem.title: INDIA: India oil stocks cheap at the price, say analysts.
newsitem.headline: India oil stocks cheap at the price, say analysts.

text.p: The prospect of capacity shortages and high demand in India's oil sector fuelling high earnings growth will attract international investors into oil stocks, analysts said on Wednesday.

"The Indian oil sector is just the sort of environment most oil sector investors have been looking for," David Gray, equity capital markets director with HSBC Investment Banking, told delegates to an international conference on Indian oil and gas.

Demand growth rates are low and there is over-capacity at most levels of the refining and marketing sector in the European and north American markets where the vast majority of quoted integrated oil firms primarily operate, Gray said.

He expected Indian demand for refind oil products to grow at an annual rate of more than six percent over the next few years. Other experts at the conference pitched the figure at around seven to eight percent.
"Given that existing assets are largely written down, the return on new investment can have a disproportionate impact on earnings growth," Gray said.
As part of divestment plans, India hopes to raise $350 million through an international equity offering in state-run refiner Indian Oil Corp (IOC), sometime during the next few months, Gray said.

Late last month, a jumbo issue of global depositary receipts by Indian telecommunications giant Videsh Sanchar Nigam Limited, was ten times oversubscribed. It raised $526.5 million, after three previous aborted launch attempts.
"For a major issue such as IOC, the major demand sources would be the USA and the UK, but we would expect significant contributions from Asia, the Middle East and Europe," he added.
Lars Reierson, a Singapore-based analyst with Morgan Stanley and Company, was similarly upbeat about the future for Indian oil stocks, but warned that investors must time their buys carefully.

"Indian shares are going to double and triple over the next few years," Reierson told Reuters. "There's going to be an enormous return on investments. It's just a question of picking the right time and the political situation."

Analysts said a definite turn-off for investors was India's huge oil pool deficit, the subsidy the government pays to state-run firms to sell their products at domestic prices that are well below international rates.
Under India's administered-pricing regime for petroleum products, it presently stands at around $4.3 billion.
"The precise workings of the oil pool deficit are a mystery to most international investors," Gray said.
"However, the idea that roughly 160 billion rupees is owed to the oil companies by a system which at present simply does not have the ability to pay is an obvious cause of concern."
An Asian Development Bank (ADB) official said the best way to deal with the oil deficit was for the government to deregulate swiftly and hasten the pace of divestment.

"They (the federal government) have to change the price regime," C.S. Chung, a senior ADB project officer, told Reuters. "We have been advising the government to move towards market-based pricing. That's the only solution."

But hastening deregulation might affect refinery economics negatively, Gray said. This along, with the prospect that the market might be flooded with a slew of oil equity in state-run firms, might drive investors away, he added.

"The market background for equity issues by the Indian oil companies is currently better than it has been for some years and we see real opportunities for other issuers to come to the market following the forthcoming IOC sale," Gray said.
